title: Could Life Start By Itself?
principle: They made amino acids — the beads that proteins are made of.

t: Every living thing you have ever seen came from another living thing. Every single one.
Every organism anyone has ever observed came from a parent organism. There are no exceptions on record — which makes the first one a genuine problem.
sub: So where did the first one come from?
Nobody knows. That is not a dodge — it is the honest state of the field, and it is agreed on all sides.

question: In 1953 two scientists put gas and water in a flask and zapped it with lightning. What came out?
Miller and Urey passed an electric discharge through a mixture of simple gases and water. What did the experiment produce?
options: Some of the building blocks that living things are made of
stages.outcome: Some of the building blocks that living things are made of
note: Have a guess. It is one of the most famous experiments there is.
Commit. Note that the popular account of this experiment and what it actually produced have drifted a long way apart.

t: They made amino acids — the beads that proteins are made of. They did not make anything alive.
The experiment produced amino acids: the components proteins are built from. It did not produce a cell, a self-copying molecule, or anything alive.

Miller–Urey demonstrated abiotic synthesis of several amino acids under assumed early-earth conditions. The gap between a mixture of monomers and a self-replicating, metabolising, information-bearing system remains open.

The result was real and important, and its popular reading is not what it showed. Producing monomers is a long way from the assembly, sequence-specificity, homochirality, compartmentation and coupled replication a minimal cell requires.
sub: Beads are not a necklace, and a necklace is not alive.
Having the parts is not the same as having the thing. Nobody has bridged that gap in a laboratory.
The leading current hypothesis is an RNA world, in which a molecule that both stores information and catalyses reactions preceded both DNA and protein. It has real support and real unsolved problems.

The RNA-world hypothesis addresses the chicken-and-egg problem of DNA needing proteins and proteins needing DNA, and it has laboratory support in ribozymes. Its difficulties — prebiotic ribose synthesis, nucleotide assembly, homochirality, and the fidelity threshold for replication — are openly discussed in the mainstream literature.

t: Everyone agrees nobody has done it. Here is what each side thinks that means.
The empirical situation is agreed: origin of life is unsolved. The disagreement is about what to conclude from an unsolved problem.
evidence: Nobody has ever made something alive from things that were not alive. Everyone agrees about that.
No laboratory has produced a self-replicating, metabolising system from non-living chemistry. This is not disputed by anybody, and the mainstream literature says so plainly.

claim: It is a hard problem that has not been solved yet, and there is no reason to think it cannot be.
This is an open research problem, not a demonstrated impossibility. Unsolved is not unsolvable.
because: Lots of hard problems looked impossible before someone solved them. Real progress has been made on pieces of it.

Individual steps have been achieved under plausible conditions: nucleotide synthesis without a prebiotic ribose step, self-replicating ribozymes, lipid vesicles that grow and divide, and mineral surfaces that concentrate and orient reactants. They argue the history of science favours continued work over declaring a boundary, and note that arguing from a current gap to a permanent one has a poor track record.
predicts: More of the steps should keep being filled in.
Incremental closure: further prebiotically-plausible synthesis routes, higher-fidelity self-replicators, and eventually coupled replication inside a compartment.

claim: Life needs instructions, and instructions do not write themselves out of chemistry.
The barrier is not chemical but informational: a living system requires specified sequence, and chemistry alone has no tendency to produce it.
because: Chemistry can make the beads. It does not tell you what order to put them in — and the order is the whole thing.

They argue the sequence in DNA is not determined by the chemistry of the backbone, so no chemical law explains why one sequence rather than another; that all known instances of specified information trace to a mind; and they point to homochirality, the instability of the required molecules, and the absence of any known route to a functional sequence as evidence that the gap is one of kind rather than degree.
predicts: The gap between chemicals and instructions should stay unclosed.
Continued failure to produce sequence specificity from undirected chemistry, and continued reliance on experimenter intervention in the successful steps.

ask: One says 'not yet'. The other says 'not ever'. How would you tell which one you are looking at?

Both accounts are consistent with today's evidence, which is a warning sign that today's evidence is not the discriminator. So ask each: what result would you accept as decisive against yourself, and how long should 'not yet' be given before it becomes an excuse? Notice that the second question cuts both ways — an argument from a present gap is only as strong as the gap is permanent.

q: Has anyone ever made something alive out of things that were not alive?
What is the current experimental status of the origin of life?
What is the honest experimental status of abiogenesis?
options: No. Some of the steps, but not the whole thing
Yes, it happens in laboratories all the time
why: The famous experiment made building blocks, not a living thing. It is still an open question, and anyone who tells you it is settled is going beyond the evidence.
Individual steps have been achieved; the whole has not. Both sides of the disagreement accept this, and a textbook or a video that implies otherwise has overstated the case.

This is worth being precise about, because it is misreported in both directions: popular accounts sometimes imply the problem is solved, and some critiques imply no progress has been made. Neither is accurate. Substantial partial results exist; a complete route does not.

t: Knowing exactly what has and has not been shown is a skill you will use everywhere.

The ability to state precisely what an experiment demonstrated, as distinct from what it is popularly taken to demonstrate, is worth more than any particular result — and it is the single most transferable thing in this module.
